The effectiveness of large models in various machine learning tasks has been well-documented, but the constraints imposed by computational limitations on the size of these models remain unclear. In this study, we examine the trade-offs between the size of a model and the learning tasks it can successfully complete under computational constraints. In the context of matrix completion, we demonstrate that, given a budget of T operations, a learner can achieve a test error rate of O(T^(-1/2)) by utilizing a model with T parameters. Furthermore, we show that, for a learner to consistently attain an optimal T^(-1/2) rate across a range of problem instances, the model must have at least T/ln(T) parameters. In contrast, we establish that, for a learner to achieve T^(-1/2) on all matrix completion instances, the model must have at least Tln(T) parameters. In addition, we investigate the computational constraints of learning from data in a sequential manner, and we establish a lower bound on the size of the model required to learn from data in this manner. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the design of large models in various machine learning tasks.

We demonstrate that within the context of a countable discrete abelian group, there exists a Bohr set that can be found within the sum of the images of a subset of the group when the images have cardinality at least $C_1(\epsilon)^k$, where $C_1(\epsilon)$ depends on $\epsilon$ and $k$ is the size of the images. This result reveals that our previous findings for the case of a $k$-free abelian group are optimal. We also show that our previous work for the case of a $k$-free abelian group is the best possible in all aspects.

As cities strive to reduce pollution and traffic, ridepooling is becoming a key solution. However, the success of ridepooling hinges on balancing high participation rates with minimal detours for passengers. Current approaches to solving this challenge rely on complex algorithms that are computationally expensive and difficult to implement in real-time. To address this issue, we propose a new, efficient algorithm called Online Ridepooling. This algorithm is designed to be fast and effective, allowing for real-time implementation. Our approach involves breaking down the ridepooling problem into smaller sub-problems and solving them using a combination of techniques. Our results show that the Online Ridepooling algorithm achieves near-optimal performance, with a performance guarantee of at least 84% of the optimal solution. This approach allows for real-time implementation and can be easily adapted to different scenarios.

This paper presents a novel approach to tackling the complexities of multi-modal data in E-commerce, which is plagued by diverse data types, insufficient training samples, and the need for data integration. Our proposed method utilizes an information-theoretic framework to capture both local and global relationships between different data modalities. By employing a novel optimization technique, we are able to derive an information-theoretic representation that is grounded in theory. Our approach is evaluated on a large real-world E-commerce dataset, which is collected from Alibaba.com, and demonstrates significant improvements in data representation and retrieval tasks. Our results also reveal that the proposed method is capable of handling a wide range of data types and is adaptable to different use cases.

A novel approach, Deep InfoMax (DIM), has been developed to enhance the analysis of brain imaging data, particularly in the context of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) diagnosis. By leveraging non-linear statistical dependencies in data, DIM has shown superior performance compared to traditional methods. In this study, DIM was applied to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data to classify children with ASD and neurotypical counterparts. The results indicate that DIM achieved a 70.5% accuracy in binary classification, outperforming existing methods. The study also highlights the effectiveness of applying DIM to multi-dimensional data, such as brain images, and its potential for future applications in neuroimaging research.

This study introduces a novel unsupervised method for identifying the most relevant text in predefined class categories. The proposed influence score (I-score) leverages the relationships between words in the data to determine the impact of each word on classification accuracy. By utilizing the BERT model, our approach achieves state-of-the-art results in the TextRank challenge, outperforming existing techniques. The I-score method demonstrates superior performance in identifying the best query to retrieve a classification of 'football', and also successfully applies to the classification of 'coronavirus'.

A theoretical model is developed to investigate the spin-orbit coupling's influence on electron correlations in a two-orbital Hubbard model with finite electron density. Calculations are performed using a mean-field approach and the self-consistent Hartree-Fock method. The study finds that when electron-electron interactions are weak, the system remains paramagnetic, but when they are strong, it becomes a magnetic insulator. Interestingly, the effective spin-orbit coupling constant is reduced in the paramagnetic phase as interactions increase, and it is also reduced in the magnetic phase. This suggests that electron-electron interactions can significantly affect spin-orbit coupling strength.

A new dark matter candidate is proposed, consisting of a complex scalar field with a specific symmetry breaking pattern. This candidate is long-lived due to its properties, and its potential allows for a viable thermal relic abundance. The candidate's characteristics enable it to be produced in experiments like the LHC and the International Linear Collider, and it can be detected through specific decay signatures.

The effectiveness of machine learning models in medical settings is often compromised by differences between training and deployment data. As a result, accurately predicting AI model performance in new environments is crucial. This study presents a method for estimating the performance of AI models in unfamiliar environments without access to relevant data. The proposed approach, based on a model of the data distribution, can identify the characteristics of unfamiliar environments and use this information to predict AI model performance. The method was tested on a dataset of chest X-rays and achieved promising results.

The most reliable method for modeling nucleic acids at an atomic level is through molecular dynamics simulations. These simulations can examine the six rotational components of the molecule, encompassing base rotations, sugar rotations, and rotations of the phosphate backbone. This study investigates the feasibility of using a simple, card-based model to accurately predict atomic-level molecule behavior. We found that molecular and atomic-level simulations of a specific DNA molecule are remarkably similar when comparing two models with vastly different complexities. This similarity suggests that molecular behavior can be effectively predicted using simplified models.

This study investigates the Reeds-Sloane initialization for Asymmetric Numeral Systems, a variant of entropy coding introduced by Duda. The paper examines the performance of this initialization in the context of the tabled Asymmetric Numeral Systems (tANS) encoder, a widely used implementation of ANS. The research reveals that the tANS encoder with Duda's precise initialization incurs a redundancy of 1/(2ln(2)) per symbol, a result that is 1/2ln(2) greater than the redundancy of the ANS with Reeds-Sloloane initialization. The study further demonstrates that the Reeds-Sloane initialization can be efficiently tabled, a finding that is relevant to entropy coding applications.

The dielectric properties of aqueous electrolyte liquids are heavily influenced by ion correlations, an effect that is inadequately addressed by current theories. We have developed a method to calculate the dielectric response of electrolyte liquids by applying a mean-field approach to a modified version of the Poisson-Boltzmann equation, which takes into account pre-existing interactions between ions. This approach is then used to derive a new dielectric function, which is subsequently applied to a model of strong ion interactions, characterized by a limited solubility of ions in the liquid. We have found that our model accurately predicts the dielectric properties of strong electrolyte liquids, as demonstrated by comparisons with experimental data for sodium chloride in water.

Our research focuses on identifying heavy-antiheavy hadronic molecules, specifically in the $B\bar B$ and $B\bar B^*$, $B^*\bar B^*$ systems, and our findings align with a broader study on such systems. Several of these molecules, including the $B\bar B^*$ pentaquark $P_{cs}(4337)$, align with the predicted spectrum. Additionally, a few more, such as the $B\bar B^*$ isospin doublets and $B^*\bar B^*$ singlet, could potentially be discovered in the future. We also explore the possible existence of $D\bar D^*$, $D^*\bar D^*$, $D_s\bar D^*_s$ systems, and our results suggest that some of these systems, including the $D_s\bar D^*_s$ system, could host a set of tetraquark states.

This study examines the evolution of swarm drones in the military sector by analyzing a comprehensive dataset of 10,918 scholarly papers sourced from the IEEE Xplore digital library. The investigation delves into the underlying causes of this technology's rapid advancement by analyzing publication trends, research focus, and the interconnections between key concepts. The findings reveal that 2019 and 2020 experienced significant breakthroughs in military swarm drones, with a notable increase in publications and a shift in research emphasis towards multi-robot systems, unmanned aerial vehicles, and signal processing. The research also highlights the critical role of these systems in the defense industry, with a growing interest in their applications for surveillance, mapping, and the integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning.

We've conducted a comprehensive analysis of the Lyman-alpha forest's 3D correlation functions to extract cosmological information. By combining data from the SDSS-III/BOSS and eBOSS surveys, we've established constraints on the amplitude of matter fluctuations and other key cosmological parameters. Our results show that incorporating the full shape of the 3D correlation function significantly tightens the constraints on the amplitude of matter fluctuations, yielding a value of A_Lya = 0.92 (+0.13, -0.10) at 68% confidence. This value is consistent with the Planck measurement, and including the full shape also significantly tightens the constraints on the Hubble constant, yielding H0 = 70.2 (+2.1, -1.9) km/s/Mpc at 68% confidence. Our analysis demonstrates that Lyman-alpha forest power spectrum data can provide valuable insights into the cosmological model, particularly in the context of the standard cosmological model.

Researchers at the Advanced Light Source have successfully implemented a new technique for emittance exchange using beam beating, which involves combining two beams with different properties. This method, demonstrated with an additional beam at the ALS, allows for the study of beam emittance through a process called emittance exchange. The experiment involved swapping the transverse beam emittance of the existing beam with that of a new beam, and measuring the results using a technique called beam imaging. The researchers observed a significant increase in the beam size of the new beam, which was consistent with the expected emittance of the original beam. This technique has several potential applications, including the development of new beam diagnostics tools and the study of beam emittance in particle accelerators.

The rapid advancement of video technology has led to an abundance of high-resolution video data, which can be used to track the movement of individuals. Video-based trajectory prediction has become a crucial area of research, with applications spanning from autonomous driving to security surveillance. Despite significant progress in this field, existing deep learning methods struggle to accurately predict the movement of individuals, particularly when they encounter obstacles. This paper presents a novel approach, which combines the strengths of deep learning and physics-based modeling to improve the accuracy of trajectory predictions. The proposed method, which we call OCP-TrajNet, involves a two-stage process. The first stage involves using a deep learning model to generate a set of possible future paths, while the second stage employs a physics-based simulator to select the most likely path. This hybrid approach allows for the incorporation of physical constraints, such as the movement of individuals around obstacles, to improve the accuracy of trajectory predictions. The results of our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing deep learning methods in terms of accuracy, particularly when predicting the movement of individuals around obstacles.

We've examined the dynamics of a specific class of randomly connected recurrent neural networks that learn through an adaptive process. The analysis focuses on neural activity and synaptic strength evolution, which we've characterized using a self-consistent approach. We've discovered that Hebbian learning leads to neural activity with a non-zero average, which in turn causes the network to develop complex behavior. We've also found that the network's behavior can be categorized into distinct phases, which we've related to the network's structure and parameters. Our findings provide a framework for understanding and predicting neural network behavior, which may have implications for the study of neural systems and machine learning.

This study presents a novel approach to controlling a swarm of robots using hand gestures captured by a depth camera. The implemented gesture recognition system leverages a modified version of the OpenPose algorithm, initially designed for detecting human skeletal structures. The gesture recognition module processes depth images to identify key skeletal points and map them to corresponding robot parameters, enabling the modulation of swarm behavior through hand poses. The effectiveness of this system was demonstrated by successfully deploying a hand gesture-based controller on a swarm of five robots, with the aim of navigating a designated target area.

The detection of white blood cells is a crucial step in diagnosing various diseases, and recent advancements in neural network-based models have shown promising results in automating this process. A study was conducted to compare the effectiveness of different white blood cell types using a dataset of 10,000 images, and the performance of these models was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score metrics.

A key issue with counterdiabatic protocols in achieving rapid state transfer in quantum systems is the significant increase in the required energy expenditure. This study introduces a new method for rapidly and efficiently transporting a quantum system's state, by combining elements of counterdiabatic protocols and adiabatic evolution. This novel approach enables the precise manipulation of a quantum system's state without necessitating excessive energy consumption, and it outperforms existing methods in both efficiency and robustness.

A substantial number of grayscale images are utilized in various applications, such as image processing and computer vision, making them a vital component in these fields. Effective management of these images is essential for tasks like image editing, colorization, and others. Grayscale images, devoid of color information, are represented using a single channel, with pixel intensity values indicating brightness levels. This research presents a novel, efficient, and effective approach for converting RGB images to grayscale, leveraging a deep learning framework. The proposed method employs a deep neural network to learn the mapping between RGB and grayscale images, thereby achieving superior performance compared to traditional linear conversion operators. The results demonstrate that the proposed deep learning-based grayscale conversion method yields improved image quality and better preserves the image's overall appearance.

We express differentiable complex-valued functions as a sum of exponentials with coefficients that depend on their Taylor expansion, then derive an expression for an integral of such a function over the interval from 0 to 1 by applying the trapezoidal rule and expanding it into a series. This expression involves the derivatives of the function and the coefficients of the Euler-Mascheroni constant expansion, allowing us to establish an expansion for the numerical approximation of the integral that can be truncated to yield an efficient algorithm for computing the integral of a differentiable function. This algorithm is efficient because it only requires the evaluation of derivatives at a single point, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by applying it to the Riemann zeta function and the error function.

Given a surface S, an almost conformal harmonic map from the 2-sphere to S, 
excluding any points where it fails to conformally map, is investigated. 
This map, excluding its points of failure, is shown to be a branched covering 
onto S, and we calculate the degree of this branched covering. 
The degree of this branched covering is the key factor in classifying the target 
surface S, and we identify specific types of surfaces that can be achieved 
by varying this degree.

The collision of laser photons with high-energy gamma rays is a promising method for studying quantum electrodynamics in extreme conditions.  A particularly important process is the creation of an electron-positron pair from two photons, which can be achieved using a high-intensity laser.  A recent experiment involving the ELI Beamlines has made significant progress in this area by successfully generating electron-positron pairs through the interaction of high-energy gamma rays and intense laser light.  Our research provides a detailed theoretical explanation of this achievement, which involved simulating the production of electron-positron pairs in experiments conducted with the European Gamma Ray Source.  Our simulations show that the generated electron-positron pairs are consistent with experimental observations, which suggests that the process is primarily due to the interaction of high-energy gamma rays and intense laser light.  Our results also suggest that future experiments involving the use of a high-energy gamma ray beam with a high-intensity laser could significantly enhance our understanding of quantum electrodynamics in extreme conditions.

This study investigates the Two Higgs Doublet Model (2HDM) in its type-I configuration, with a primary focus on the parameter space that can be constrained by the LHC experiments. The research aims to identify areas of the parameter space that are not yet bounded by existing data, with a particular emphasis on the influence of the parameter $m_{12}$ on the model's phenomenology. The study reveals that for $m_{12}$ values below 100 GeV, the model's predictions are largely independent of $m_{12}$, with the two-higgsless scenario closely mirroring that of the Minimal Standard Model (MSM). The research also highlights the importance of considering the mass of the charged Higgs ($m_A$) in understanding the model's behavior. The findings suggest that for $m_A$ values below 100 GeV, the model's predictions are largely unaffected by variations in $m_{12}$. The research further demonstrates that the model's predictions are most sensitive to variations in the mass of the pseudoscalar Higgs ($m_P$) in the mass range of 100-500 GeV. The study's conclusions are based on a detailed analysis of the model's predictions in relation to the latest LHC experiments, with a particular focus on the detection of additional scalar particles. The research's findings have significant implications for the understanding of the Standard Model and the potential for discovering new scalar

We have developed a relational data exchange framework that leverages RDF data, by integrating typed IRI constructors into the relational setting. This allows us to establish a bidirectional mapping between RelRDF and its source relations. Our framework, which is defined over RelRDF, includes data exchange instances that can be represented in the source-target language. We have shown that this framework is capable of encoding a wide range of RelRDF target expressions, including those generated by RDF graph pattern queries. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the applicability of our framework to RDF data exchange by providing a data exchange instance that captures the expressive power of SPARQL-based RDF data exchange.

Recent advancements in regional science have led to the incorporation of non-parametric and parametric methods for productivity and efficiency analysis, as well as the regression of these measures. This paper explores the latest developments in these areas, with a focus on the underlying assumptions and limitations of these new techniques. It also highlights potential applications and challenges, ultimately providing a comprehensive overview of these rapidly evolving methodologies.

We suggest a new method for reconstructing scalar boson production with low masses at the LHC, utilizing a machine learning approach to enhance mass resolution and improve sensitivity to new physics. By incorporating a resolution term into the likelihood function, our method achieves better mass resolution and higher signal sensitivity. As an example, our approach can increase mass resolution for Higgs boson production by a factor of 2.5 and improve signal sensitivity by 20% in a specific search for low mass Higgs bosons decaying into a pair of W bosons.

We investigate the syntactic parsing capabilities of pre-trained language models, specifically examining the information within their self-attention mechanisms. We discovered that the attention matrices can be used to identify the syntactic structure of sentences. We hypothesized that the parsing information is not directly encoded in the attention matrices, but rather that the information is encoded in the linear projection matrices that generate these matrices. We found that the projection matrices for queries and keys are highly correlated with a set of learned matrices that can be used to accurately predict a dependency tree. We also found that the correlation between the learned matrices and the attention matrices is negligible. We further demonstrated that the dependency structure of sentences can be inferred from the projection matrices.

This study assesses the effectiveness of combining different datasets for training German automatic speech recognition models. We compare the performance of models trained on the ARANEWS and SPKENWP datasets, as well as Araneus' integrated dataset, Araneus+WP. Experiments were conducted on the WSJ-MD benchmark, and results indicate that models trained on the combined dataset significantly outperform the others, with a 10% improvement in accuracy over the ARANEWS-only dataset.

Our research involves a comprehensive analysis of 100 Be-type stars, a subset of the larger collection of 120 Be stars within the Local Bubble, utilizing data from the Gaia Data Release 2. By examining their radial velocities, we've determined the orbital motions of these stars, and through a statistical approach, we've identified their membership in the Local Bubble. Additionally, we've calculated the rotational velocities of their companion stars, finding that Be stars rotate faster than their B-type counterparts. Our findings also reveal that the Local Bubble contains a higher concentration of thick disk stars, a trend that is reflected in the distribution of these stars' metallicities.

This research investigates the application of inverse text normalization (ITN) in the context of automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. The study compares the effectiveness of ITN models developed using either a hand-crafted or an integrated ASR-based approach. The experiment involved a dataset of $1000$ speech samples collected from native English speakers, which were converted into corresponding numerical values. The findings indicate that the ASR-based ITN model significantly outperforms the hand-crafted ITN model in terms of accuracy, achieving a $99.9\%$ rate of correct speech-to-text conversion.

We demonstrate a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, showing that the optimal domain is a ball, in contrast to previous studies that addressed Dirichlet or Neumann boundary conditions. The proof relies on the use of the magnetic Faber-Krahn inequality and the magnetic Wirtinger inequality derived from a carefully chosen vector field.

Deep neural networks have become a standard in medical imaging, but their complexity poses a major challenge for understanding their behavior and interpreting their results. This issue is particularly prevalent in medical imaging, where a lack of interpretability can hinder their adoption. To address this, researchers have developed various methods to interpret deep neural networks, but these methods are often limited in their scope and applicability. A new approach has been proposed to address this issue by providing a comprehensive and efficient way to interpret deep neural networks. This method, called LIFT, uses a novel technique to identify and visualize the features that drive a model's predictions. By doing so, LIFT can help researchers and practitioners gain a deeper understanding of how deep neural networks work and how they can be improved.

One-dimensional non-Hermitian systems with open boundaries exhibit striking characteristics, including exceptional points and striking color patterns, which are heavily influenced by correlations. We investigate the impact of correlations on the topological classification of these systems, discovering that correlations can significantly alter the topological properties. A model with long-range interactions is analyzed, showing that the emergence of a non-Bloch skin mode is contingent upon a specific condition related to interaction strength. Furthermore, the presence of short-range interactions can lead to a transition between distinct phases, which is accompanied by a change in the system's boundary spectrum and a shift in the topological phase.

This study examines the acoustic characteristics of warmth in synthetic speech,
aiming to enhance the development of more natural-sounding speech synthesis
techniques. To achieve this goal, we examine the effects of warmth on the
perceived gender of synthetic speech and investigate the acoustic markers of
warmth. Our analysis involves a listening experiment to gather human feedback
and employs statistical analysis to identify the most significant acoustic
features contributing to warmth. The results indicate that the presence of
formant frequencies in the lower range of the spectrum is a crucial factor in
creating the perception of warmth.

A radiative seesaw model incorporating a global $U(1)_X$ symmetry has been developed to address the issues of neutrino mass and dark matter simultaneously. The model proposes that neutrino masses are generated at the two-loop level, with a dark matter candidate that is stable due to the conservation of $U(1)_X$. The model's framework is based on a specific set of particles, with the gauge group $SU(3)_C \otimes SU(2)_L \otimes U(1)_Y \otimes U(1)_X$. The analysis of the radiative seesaw mechanism reveals that the dark matter candidate's mass range is between $10^4$ GeV and $10^{11}$ GeV, with a corresponding $U(1)_X$ breaking scale of $10^5$ GeV to $10^7$ GeV. The model's framework is further constrained by perturbative unitarity, with the $U(1)_X$ gauge coupling remaining below $0.3$ and the $U(1)_X$ gauge boson's mass range is between $10^4$ GeV and $10^7$ GeV. The model's framework is also consistent with the dark matter relic density and its direct and indirect detection limits, with a specific focus on the annihilation of dark matter into $U(1)_X$ gauge bosons. The model's framework

In the context of the Bohr-Mottelson model, the concept of minimal length finds a natural geometric interpretation for even-even nuclei with an $N=8$ neutron subshell closure. The application of the Kruppa potential to the even-even $^{152}$Dy and $^{154}$Dy isotopes reveals a notable minimum minimal length at $N=16$ for both, indicating a shared underlying mechanism. The study further explores the implications of this phenomenon on the system's phase space and its transition from discrete to continuous energy states.

This paper presents a novel approach to omnidirectional precoding by utilizing Golay complementary matrices, which enables the reduction of inter-user interference in downlink transmissions. The proposed Golay CP system offers a more flexible framework for Golay complementary precoding, allowing for adjustable CP length and flexible subcarrier spacing. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the sum of squared channel estimation errors is minimized in the Golay CP system, resulting in optimal performance. The results show that the Golay CP system achieves a lower bit error rate compared to conventional channel estimation methods, particularly in scenarios with low signal-to-noise ratios. The proposed Golay CP system is also found to be more robust to Doppler shift effects, offering a potential solution for omnidirectional precoding in mobile communication systems.

This paper introduces an innovative approach for detecting changes in multi-spectral images using a deep convolutional autoencoder with feature fusion capabilities. The proposed method combines local and global features from a multi-scale local convolutional block and a global convolutional block, which are then encoded and reconstructed using a multi-scale convolutional decoder. The changes in the image are identified by analyzing the reconstruction error between the original image and its reconstructed form. The multi-scale structure of the network allows for the extraction of features at various levels, which are then used to improve the network's performance. The proposed method has been tested on three datasets and has shown superior results compared to existing methods.

We have conducted a comprehensive examination of the residual entropy concept, initially introduced by Rosenfeld in 1975, and its numerous applications in understanding fluid behavior. Our analysis focused on the correlation between residual entropy and key properties such as viscosity, thermal conductivity, and dielectric relaxation, and its role in developing predictive models for fluid dynamics. Additionally, we investigated the effects of molecular shape and structure on these correlations, and their potential applications in predicting complex fluid behavior. Our research also explored the use of residual entropy in studying mixtures and their properties, and the challenges associated with applying this concept to mixtures. Ultimately, we found that the residual entropy concept has significant potential in predicting and explaining fluid behavior, and its applications continue to expand as new insights and experimental data become available.

A novel periodic cosmology is proposed, in which the universe's expansion is driven by alternating phases of dark energy and dust, with the transition between these phases governed by a specific condition. This approach is grounded in the hypothesis that the universe's evolution is influenced by a quantum mechanical system, whose wave function's behavior is described by a Schrödinger equation. A key aspect of this model is the assumption that the universe's evolution is analogous to a quantum system's behavior, with the wave function's probability distribution guiding the dynamics. This analogy is further explored by relating the Schrödinger equation to a parabolic partial differential equation, with the resulting dynamics being influenced by the wave function's probability distribution. This approach is further developed by relating the probability distribution to the universe's energy density, with the resulting dynamics being governed by a new equation. This new equation is found to be consistent with the Friedmann equations, with the resulting dynamics being analogous to the universe's evolution in a standard cosmological model. This model is further developed by relating the probability distribution to the universe's scale factor, with the resulting dynamics being analogous to the universe's evolution in a standard cosmological model. A superdeterministic explanation for quantum mechanics, particularly in relation to Bell correlations, has been a contentious issue. A notable proposal, the tetrodynamics model, claims to offer a superdeterministic account of quantum mechanics, drawing parallels with tetravector calculus in classical electromagnetism. However, the validity of this model is disputed due to its failure to replicate Bell correlations, a problem that persists even with modifications to the tetrodynamics model. An alternative, the trigavector model, presents itself as a superdeterministic model that can account for Bell correlations. It is argued that this model is the correct approach, as it is the only one that can provide a superdeterministic explanation for Bell correlations.

This study presents an innovative approach to developing a highly efficient
convolutional neural network (CNN) for keyword spotting on resource-constrained
IoT devices. The proposed model, called TinyKS, is specifically designed to
operate within the limited memory constraints of embedded systems. To achieve
this goal, TinyKS incorporates a novel method for reducing the size of
convolutional kernels, thereby decreasing the model's memory footprint.
Moreover, TinyKS employs a novel technique for minimizing the number of
multiplications required during inference, thereby enhancing its computational
performance. As a result, TinyKS exhibits exceptional performance in keyword
spotting tasks, surpassing state-of-the-art methods while requiring significantly
less memory and computational resources.

The partition function for a two-dimensional Dirac field in the presence of a gauge field is studied within a specific framework of connections between fermionic and random matrix theories. This study focuses on the part of the partition function that remains unchanged under gauge transformations. It is demonstrated that this invariant part of the partition function can be expressed as a sum of products of determinants, a result that is analogous to the Atiyah-Patodi-Singer index theorem. Additionally, the study reveals that each term in this expression corresponds to a fermionic version of a specific matrix model, a result that is analogous to the Brezin-Hikami formula.

Model or feature selection in the presence of categorical data is particularly challenging due to issues with identifiability and the lack of a well-established approach. To address this difficulty, we developed a novel sparse modeling technique for categorical data, dubbed Lasso with Augmented Weighted Triangularization (LAWT), which is capable of handling sparse modeling or model selection tasks in the presence of categorical data. LAWT is an optimization-based method that transforms the problem into a linear programming task, making it a versatile tool for feature selection. To further improve its performance, we developed an efficient algorithm for updating the Lagrange multipliers, resulting in a faster solution. To evaluate its effectiveness, we conducted experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets, demonstrating that LAWT outperforms existing approaches in sparse modeling or model selection tasks involving categorical data.

Embedded real-time systems often require isolation and virtualization, but traditional hypervisors can introduce excessive latency, making them unsuitable for mixed criticality systems. To address this issue, we propose T-Visor, a T-Engine based virtualization layer that provides real-time guarantees for high-priority guest tasks. By implementing T-Visor on an industrial-grade T-Engine 2 SoC, we were able to achieve T-Visor's TID scheduler, which ensures T-Visor guests receive dedicated CPU time slices, resulting in T-Visor guests meeting their deadlines with 100% accuracy. Furthermore, we were able to achieve T-Visor guests meeting their deadlines with 100% accuracy, even in the presence of other T-Visor guests with lower priority requirements.

This research demonstrates that panoramic image quality can be significantly degraded by camera tilt, which results in geometric distortion. To address this issue, we developed an innovative method for stitching tilted panoramic images, which incorporates an optimization technique to simultaneously determine the camera's orientation and a set of control points representing the camera's tilt. The camera's rotation axis is fixed, and our approach yields an efficient and computationally effective solution. The results show that this method surpasses existing solutions in terms of accuracy, which is further validated by both experimental and real-world data.

In networks of oscillators with multiple distinct populations, a phenomenon called complete bipartite synchrony arises, where two populations exhibit synchronized and asynchronous behavior respectively. This research investigates the conditions under which complete bipartite synchrony occurs in coupled oscillators with different natural frequencies and parameters. By using a mathematical approach, the study derives a set of inequalities that determine the existence of complete bipartite synchrony in bipartite networks of oscillators. These inequalities are based on the eigenvalues of the Laplacian matrix and the parameters of the oscillators. The study also provides a method for determining the maximum and minimum values of the parameters that lead to complete bipartite synchrony. The findings of the study are verified through numerical simulations.

We investigate the effectiveness of model-based reinforcement learning algorithms, which can anticipate future states and optimize policies more efficiently than their model-free counterparts. However, the model-based approach is susceptible to inaccuracies in the learned dynamics model. We propose a novel, model-based offline policy learning algorithm that leverages offline data to predict future states and improve the policy. Our method outperforms the offline variant of the powerful, on-policy actor-critic algorithm PPO in the stochastic control of nonlinear systems and the Atari game Breakout.

We develop multi-layer quivers with labels to create infinite-type algebras of a specific form, which can be used to investigate the isomorphism problem for quiver algebras. The concept is applied to the algebras of path and walk, and we solve the isomorphism problem for path algebras of multi-layer quivers. Additionally, we demonstrate that an appropriate family of walk algebras is distinct from one another up to isomorphism.

We examine the behavior of reflected entropy in holographic field theories, specifically focusing on how it deviates from random tensor networks near the AdS boundary. Our investigation reveals that the kth bisymmetric extension of reduced density matrices for the region B and its complement A exhibits similar patterns to those of the corresponding density matrices. Furthermore, the nonaveraged cross-ratios inherent in Rényi and Rényi entropies, as well as the bisymmetric extensions, are found to be expressible in terms of specific correlation functions within the CFT. Our results also demonstrate that the nonaveraged cross-ratios, as defined by Fubini-Study metrics for the eigenstates of the reduced density matrices, can be calculated using the HRT surface in the bulk AdS space. Our study also reveals that the nonaveraged cross-ratios can be expressed as the expectation values of the star-shaped four-point function, as well as the expectation values of the product of two Virasoro block functions, which are determined by the HRT surface in the bulk AdS space. Our research also shows that the nonaveraged cross-ratios can be expressed as the expectation values of the star-shaped four-point function, as well as the expectation values of the product of two Virasoro block functions, which are determined by the HRT surface in the bulk AdS space. The concept of maximum likelihood estimation is used to identify the most probable state of a system at any given time, taking into account its history. This is particularly useful in analyzing complex systems that evolve over time, such as those that are constantly changing and unpredictable. By applying this technique to a system that is in a steady state, researchers can determine the likelihood of different states and identify patterns that persist over time. They found that systems with a higher rate of change tend to have shorter-lived patterns, while those with lower rates of change have more persistent patterns. This has implications for understanding and predicting complex systems that are in a steady state.

We investigate the dynamics of a two-body system in a plane, where one body is constrained to move within that plane and is subject to a central force. This force is central and conservative, and its potential is an arbitrary function of the distance between the bodies. We demonstrate that the dynamical system exhibits chaotic behavior, and we identify and categorize the specific types of chaotic orbits. We also investigate and discuss the conditions under which these chaotic orbits occur.

The gravitational gauge theory known as the double copy has significant implications in theoretical physics, linking gauge theories and gravity theories. This relationship has been further explored by the gravitational-scalar-photon (GSP) framework, which successfully combines gravity, scalar fields, and photons. This framework has now been expanded to the GSP with double copy, which establishes a connection between a new class of ${\cal N}=2$ supergravity theories and bi-adjoint scalar theory coupled with abelian gauge theory and ${\cal N}=1$ vector multiplet. This novel correspondence is supported by explicit examples and further validated through the derivation of its underlying principles.

We investigate the statistical behavior of specific classes of hook lengths in partition shapes, demonstrating through an analytical approach that these lengths exhibit normal distribution patterns when n is scaled by a factor of the square root. This finding is further generalized to other partition shapes, including those defined by Durfee triangles and Rhomboid diagrams, and we also examine the shapes formed by concatenating multiple partitions.

Our research investigates the time taken for a quantum particle to tunnel through a potential barrier in the context of the Landau-Zener model. The particle, initially in a superposition of two states, experiences a magnetic field that causes its spin to precess as it approaches the barrier. The time taken for this process is determined by the rate of change of the external parameter driving the system. The measurement of tunneling time is made possible by the change in the particle's state after it has passed through the barrier, which can be observed through the probability of detecting the particle in a specific state. The results of our study show that the particle's tunneling time is influenced by the parameters of the Landau-Zener model and that it can be used to study the quantum properties of the system.

We've developed a universal function to describe the momentum distribution of non-relativistic mesons with angular momentum of one unit. This function is used to generate the form factors of these mesons. Our research specifically focuses on type-II P-wave non-relativistic mesons, which are composed of quarks and anti-quarks. We've derived the form factors for these mesons by combining the universal function with the wave function describing their bound state. We've also made direct comparisons between our theoretical model and the results of lattice QCD simulations.

Research in quantum information processing and interferometry has heavily relied on quantum mechanics principles. However, the possibility of nonlinear quantum mechanics remains an open question. Our research explores the potential impact of nonlinearity on quantum states, particularly in relation to phase estimation accuracy. By examining the phase operator's Heisenberg equation of motion, we found that nonlinearity can lead to the phase operator becoming non-Hermitian, resulting in an uncertain phase. Consequently, this would hinder the achievement of the quantum limit in phase estimation. Our findings indicate that the phase estimation quantum limit is not feasible in nonlinear quantum mechanics, which would also pose challenges to the development of quantum technologies in this field.

Recent research has shown that the asymptotic symmetries of asymptotically flat spacetimes can be used to derive a quantum gravity S matrix. This approach is based on connecting the asymptotic symmetries to the Ward identities that govern the behavior of correlation functions. Specifically, the symmetry algebra of the superrotations, which is a subalgebra of the extended BMS algebra, has been identified as a $W_{1+\infty}$ algebra. This paper aims to explore the implications of this connection by developing a corresponding action for the asymptotic symmetries. This action is a light-cone metric theory, which is a type of gravity theory that is invariant under superrotations. This theory is based on a gravity theory that is invariant under the Poincaré group. By analyzing the asymptotic behavior of the action, we find that it is consistent with the expectations of the asymptotic symmetries. This result provides a new perspective on the relationship between the asymptotic symmetries and the quantum gravity S matrix.

The challenge of learning multiple tasks without forgetting previous knowledge is a significant issue in artificial intelligence.   Although there are several approaches to address this problem, they are limited by the need for multiple passes through the data or the use of external memory systems.

This framework is based on a set of functions that satisfy a system of partial differential equations. By utilizing this framework, a specific type of geometric object, the connection coefficients, can be calculated. In this research, several categories of permutation polynomials for the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q^3}$ are presented and proven, with one category dependent on the size of $q$. Additionally, new and existing families of these permutation polynomials are examined and compared, with additional properties and classifications of these polynomials for even and odd $q$ provided.

Infectious intestinal parasites pose a significant threat to human health worldwide, with millions of people affected annually. These parasites can lead to severe health complications, including diarrhea, abdominal pain, and even death. Recent advances in molecular biology have made it possible to rapidly and accurately identify these parasites. However, the high cost of these methods has limited their use. A new, cost-effective method using smartphone technology and a deep learning model has been developed to rapidly and accurately detect intestinal parasites in fecal samples. The method involves capturing images of feces and parasite eggs using a smartphone, which are then analyzed by a deep learning model. The model has been trained on a dataset of 10,000 images and has achieved an accuracy of 95% in parasite detection. The method has been tested in a clinical setting and has shown promising results. The method has the potential to revolutionize the diagnosis of intestinal parasitic infections, especially in resource-limited settings.

This study examines a stochastic investment and reinsurance game under limited short sales conditions, where both proportional and excess-of-loss reinsurance contracts are considered. The players' control variables include the proportions and limits of reinsurance, as well as the amount invested in a risky asset. By employing dynamic programming principles and the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations, we derive closed-form solutions for Nash equilibrium strategies and corresponding expected utilities. Furthermore, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of these solutions as the risk aversion of the insured approaches infinity, revealing a phenomenon where the insured's optimal strategy converges to that of a fully protected player, while the reinsurer's strategy converges to that of a player with no reinsuring ability.

This study presents a novel Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accelerated (PIDA) controller for enhancing quadcopter flight stability. The proposed controller is designed to counteract the effects of time delays in the quadcopter system. To achieve this, the PIDA controller is combined with a first-order plus time delay model, which is derived from the quadcopter's transfer function. The effectiveness of the PIDA controller is demonstrated through both theoretical analysis and simulation, which shows that it outperforms the traditional Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller in the presence of time delays. The results of the comparison indicate that the PIDA controller significantly improves quadcopter stability and tracking accuracy.

Pion-nucleon interactions at low energies are effectively described by chiral effective field theory, which is a fundamental framework in nuclear physics.  Expanding upon this, a new approach has been developed to model complex many-body systems, incorporating a density-dependent potential that depends on the local density of these systems.  This novel PNNR force potential is derived from the local density matrix and is a key component in the study of nuclear matter.  By applying this new potential to the study of nuclear matter, researchers have found that it can accurately reproduce experimental data on the local density of nucleons, particularly in the study of neutron-rich matter.  Furthermore, a new method has been developed to calculate the equation of state for neutron-rich matter, which is a key component in the study of compact stars and other astrophysical phenomena.  This new approach has found applications in the study of neutron stars and other compact objects, where precise calculations of the equation of state are essential for understanding their properties and behavior.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is a key component of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) experiment, and its silicon pixel detector plays a vital role in the tracking system. This silicon pixel detector is responsible for generating a large amount of data, and its primary function is to locate interaction points and track charged particles. As a result, the data processing pipeline must be highly efficient to handle the generated data. This paper outlines the latest developments in the CMS offline reconstruction system, specifically focusing on the hit-finding algorithm and its integration into the reconstruction system.

Our research involves a comprehensive morphological analysis of 100,000 Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) hosts, spanning redshifts from 0.001 to 3.0, based on the Galaxy Zoo database. Utilizing the NED system, we categorize these hosts into four distinct morphological types: spiral, irregular, elliptical, and elliptical/spheroidal galaxies. Our findings reveal that approximately 60% of these hosts are classified as spiral galaxies, 15% are irregular, 15% are elliptical, and 10% are elliptical/spheroidal galaxies. Additionally, we discovered that the proportion of spiral galaxies among AGN hosts decreases as redshift increases, while the proportion of elliptical galaxies increases. Our analysis also reveals that AGN occurrence is more prevalent in the outer regions of galaxies, with the likelihood of hosting an AGN decreasing with increasing galaxy radius. Our results are in line with previous studies, which have also observed a similar trend.

The high kinetic energy observed in nuclei is attributed to short-range correlations (SRC) occurring between nucleons. The SRC phenomenon, prevalent at nucleon-nucleon interaction strengths, results in nuclear wave functions exhibiting distinct high-momentum components. The SRC-induced high-momentum nucleons contribute to the nuclear kinetic energy, thereby influencing the nuclear equation of state. The SRC effect is also responsible for the nuclear symmetry energy, which plays a crucial role in determining the neutron skin thickness of heavy nuclei. The neutron skin thickness is a measure of the excess neutrons present in nuclei, which can be observed in heavy-ion collisions. The SRC effect is further reflected in the in-medium modification of nucleon properties, which can be measured through various experimental techniques. The SRC effect is a crucial factor in understanding the behavior of nuclear matter under extreme conditions, thereby contributing to the development of nuclear physics.

This paper presents a new approach to complex-valued neural networks, where the complex scaling property is exploited to create an infinite representation learning capacity. We demonstrate that complex scaling can be integrated into the backpropagation algorithm, and this method can be applied to the complex-valued Fourier transform. Our approach is tested on a complex-valued image classification task, and the results show that complex scaling can be used to create more compact models.

The non-linear QCD evolution equations are explored in relation to saturation momentum $q_s(x)$, a critical parameter in high-energy processes. When $q_s(x)$ is expressed as $x_0/x$, it simplifies the analysis and allows for the derivation of universal saturation curves for various observables. These universal curves are then applied to understand the behavior of these variables in different kinematic regions.

We analyzed the [X/Fe] abundance ratios of 109 metal-poor subgiant stars from the GALAH survey, focusing on elements such as Na, Mg, Si, Ca, Ti, and others. By excluding outliers, we determined the intrinsic scatter of these elements, which ranged from 0.07 to 0.17 dex. We then compared our findings to previous studies, which showed varying levels of scatter. Our results suggest that the [X/Fe] abundance ratios of these elements are relatively uniform, with the exception of Na, which exhibited a higher scatter. We also investigated the relationship between the [X/Fe] abundance ratios and metallicity, which revealed a weak correlation for some elements and a stronger correlation for others.

Machine learning predictions can be severely compromised when crucial information is missing, a common issue in real-world applications. The underlying cause of this problem is often the absence of a key, unobserved variable that significantly affects the outcome. The variable selection process in such scenarios is complicated by the fact that including irrelevant variables can be equally detrimental as omitting the missing variable that influences the outcome. The causal impact of unobserved variables on the performance of machine learning models is often overlooked in the existing literature. This study aims to develop a method for quantifying the causal impact of unobserved variables on prediction accuracy. The proposed method is based on the concept of relevance and incorporates the use of machine learning models to identify the missing variable that has the greatest influence on the outcome. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this method in a simulation and shows that it can successfully recover the missing variable that has the greatest influence on the outcome in various scenarios.

We introduce a novel Hybrid Quantum-Classical algorithm, specifically designed for the VQE method, to tackle classification issues. This approach leverages a Quantum Circuit to produce a non-linear decision boundary by utilizing kernel functions. A QUBO problem is then formulated, where the circuit's parameters and a classifier's coefficients are optimized using a classical solver. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations on two datasets, showing its ability to achieve high accuracy with minimal circuit depth and gate operations.

Researchers have investigated pointwise slant submanifolds within almost Hermitian manifolds, specifically focusing on their embeddings into product manifolds with Lorentzian and Riemannian components. They have derived constraints on these pointwise slant submanifolds, as well as identified conditions for null slant and totally null slant embeddings. Additionally, the study has revealed that certain types of pointwise slant submanifolds, such as Riemannian slant and null slant, cannot occur in product manifolds with specific geometries.

The development of sensitive nuclear recoil detectors is crucial for a range of important scientific applications, including dark matter detection, double beta decay research, and geoneutrino detection, all of which rely on precise low-energy nuclear recoil detection. A new type of detector, known as a liquid scintillator-based coherent neutrino neutrino nucleoscorer, has been proposed and is being developed for a wide variety of nuclear recoil applications. A prototype of this detector, called LSC-CRaN, has been successfully tested and demonstrated the ability to accurately identify nuclear recoil events and distinguish them from electron interactions. The experiment's results show that LSC-CRaN detectors can achieve a high level of sensitivity and accuracy in low-energy nuclear recoil detection, making them a promising technology for a range of important scientific applications.

We examine a model of active colloidal dimers, consisting of two beads connected by a spring, moving through a fluid with an activity gradient. This setup leads to two distinct responses: the dimers either align or orient themselves along the gradient. We find that each bead in the dimers can be treated as point particles with an effective interaction and temperature, which vary according to the activity. This allows us to derive an analytical expression for the steady-state density distribution of active dimers. This expression is then used to investigate the characteristics of active dimers, including their alignment and orientation order parameters, as well as the effect of temperature and interaction strength on these properties.

We've conducted a comprehensive study of the quantum Hall states at $1/3$, $2/7$, $2/9$, and $3/11$ densities in bilayer systems under a perpendicular magnetic field and an out-of-plane electric field. We've found that the magnetoroton dispersion curves for the $2/7$ and $2/9$ Jain states differ from those of $1/3$ or near half filling, where the magnetoroton minimum is at $k=0$. We've also discovered that the lowest energy excitation at $2/7$ and $2/9$ densities exhibits characteristics of a dipole-like excitation, which we've linked to a dipole moment generated by the bilayer dipole. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that the magnetoroton minimum at $2/9$ density is located at $k=0$ and exhibits a finite curvature, which we've attributed to the bilayer dipole.

Epidemic outbreaks are a pressing concern in our interconnected world, and understanding their spread is crucial for effective control measures. By dividing affected populations into distinct groups, researchers can pinpoint the initial infection points and predict how outbreaks will develop. This process can be particularly valuable in situations where implementing control measures is difficult or costly, allowing for targeted interventions. A novel method has been developed to analyze complex networks and identify subgroups within them, which can then be used to model the spread of diseases. This algorithm, known as KCL, utilizes a combination of clustering and centrality measures to identify distinct groups within a network, and has been shown to be highly effective in predicting the spread of diseases in both simulated and real-world scenarios.

The maximum likelihood estimator for solving the likelihood problem in CMB map-making is typically based on an approximation of the noise covariance matrix, which is derived from the periodogram method. This estimator is accurate as long as the underlying model closely matches reality. However, discrepancies between the model and actual data can lead to biased results. This bias is particularly pronounced when the model underestimates the true noise, which is often the case due to unaccounted model errors. These errors can arise from various sources, such as inaccuracies in detector simulations, flawed gain and offset calculations, or unaccounted for instrumental issues. To address this limitation, we have developed an iterative method that refines the estimator by iteratively updating the noise covariance matrix. This method is grounded in an iterative approach to solving the periodogram-based covariance problem, which is known to be biased in the presence of non-Gaussian data. By incorporating this method, we can mitigate the bias caused by model errors and achieve more accurate results.

Effective communication between a teacher and a learner is hindered by referential ambiguity, where the information being taught can be interpreted in multiple ways. To address this challenge, we've developed a novel framework for teaching concepts that can be interpreted in multiple ways. The framework relies on the assumption that the teacher aims to convey the correct interpretation of the concept, and the learner aims to grasp the correct interpretation as well. To achieve this, we've created a new type of contract, known as the Bayesian Rational Contract, which specifies the information the teacher should share to ensure the learner can accurately grasp the concept. To verify the effectiveness of this framework, we've conducted experiments using the Boardgame Game, a game that involves teaching concepts about boardgame states. The results show that this framework can help the teacher and learner communicate more effectively, even when the concepts being taught are ambiguous.

Quantum process tomography is a vital technique in quantum computing and precision sensing, allowing for the characterization of quantum processes. This process involves reconstructing a quantum channel, a mathematical representation of a quantum operation, by analyzing the outcomes of specific measurements performed on prepared quantum states. However, the full tomography method is often impractical due to the exponential increase in measurements required as the number of quantum systems increases. To address this issue, researchers have developed efficient methods to recover quantum processes by focusing on the most significant components of the operation, thereby reducing the number of measurements needed. These methods, however, have limitations, such as the need for prior knowledge of the process or the inability to handle noisy data. To overcome these limitations, a new approach has been developed that combines the advantages of previous methods, such as the use of prior knowledge and the ability to handle noisy data, while also providing a rigorous mathematical framework for the reconstruction process. This new approach, called the quantum channel sparsification method, has been shown to achieve high accuracy in simulations, even in the presence of noise and limited data.

This study aims to determine precise upper limits for the Cheeger constant in convex shapes within a two-dimensional plane. We demonstrate that the limits are determined by the shape's area, perimeter, and curvature, and that these limits are also applicable in three-dimensional shapes.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have the potential to provide cost-effective and flexible communication solutions in areas lacking infrastructure or experiencing outages. However, conventional fixed-wing UAVs are hindered by limited endurance due to their high power consumption. This paper explores the application of a novel flight strategy that leverages energy from the Earth's atmospheric conditions to extend the endurance of fixed-wing UAVs. The proposed strategy involves controlling the orientation of the rotor blades to generate additional lift, and optimizing the flight path to maximize energy absorption. The results demonstrate that this approach can significantly increase the flight time of a UAV, and that it can be applied to a variety of flight scenarios.

We investigate the influence of low-energy short-range electronic interactions in a bilayer graphene system. These interactions lead to a local scattering process that generates a momentum-dependent mass in the system's effective Hamiltonian. This mass affects the system's electronic structure, resulting in a pseudogap and a renormalization of the system's low-energy behavior. The local scattering process can be understood as a self-energy correction, which generates a mass term in the system's effective Hamiltonian. This mass term affects the system's low-energy behavior, leading to a mass renormalization. The mass renormalization is affected by the system's interaction strength, leading to a mass renormalization factor. The mass renormalization factor is calculated using a self-consistent equation, which is solved to determine the system's low-energy behavior. The system's low-energy behavior is characterized by a mass renormalization factor, which is calculated using a self-consistent equation, which is solved to determine the system's low-energy behavior. The system's low-energy behavior is characterized by a mass renormalization factor, which is calculated using a self-consistent equation, which is solved to determine the system's low-energy behavior.

This research examines the electronic properties of Sc2TbN@C80 and its derivatives, specifically the C60 and C80 forms, using computational methods. The findings reveal that the molecular orbitals of these compounds are primarily formed by the C60 or C78H18 cage, with a workfunction that is influenced by the presence of a cage. The derivatives exhibit a reduced workfunction compared to the parent compound, with the most significant reduction occurring in the C60H2 derivative. The compounds exhibit unique optical properties, with absorption peaks that are determined by the transition energies between molecular orbitals. Theoretical predictions suggest that Sc2TbN@C60H2 is a direct bandgap semiconductor, with a bandgap of 2.11 eV. The study highlights the importance of these compounds in the development of new materials for optoelectronics and other applications.

The Internet of Things (IoT) encompasses a vast array of devices, ranging from sophisticated to highly sophisticated, with advanced capabilities.  However, IoT's vast array of devices, with advanced capabilities, pose significant security risks.  To mitigate these risks, devices employ robust encryption algorithms.  Unfortunately, conventional algorithms are unsuitable for low-powered devices due to their high power consumption.  To address this issue, a novel lightweight encryption algorithm has been developed, combining bitwise and arithmetic operations to enhance security.  The algorithm has been tested using a variety of datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in terms of key sensitivity, entropy, and other factors.  The results show that the algorithm is a viable solution for IoT's security needs.

Achieving high measurement efficiency in Ramsey measurements for qubits is crucial for enhancing their performance. The efficiency of these measurements is influenced by the width of the distribution of initial qubit states. The standard Ramsey measurement technique, which uses a single measurement duration, may not be optimal for all qubit states. To address this limitation, we propose an innovative approach that involves taking multiple measurements with varying durations and combining the results. This approach allows us to determine the optimal measurement duration for each qubit state, thereby maximizing the information gained from each measurement. The efficiency of these combined measurements is evaluated using the quantum Fisher information and the Bayesian Cramer-Rao bound. The results demonstrate that our approach can significantly improve the measurement efficiency, particularly for qubit states with small initial amplitudes. The approach is also applied to the Blandino et al. measurement scheme, which uses a single measurement duration, and the results show that our approach can significantly improve the efficiency of these measurements.

Network centrality metrics assess the significance of nodes within a network.
This study reexamines the Gromov centrality metric, which evaluates a node's
prominence based on the average triangle inequality excess formed by the node
and pairs of other nodes in the network. We demonstrate that the triangle
inequality excess can be broken down into two distinct components, one of which
is directly related to the graph distance between nodes, while the other is
referred to as the residual excess. We show that the residual excess is
connected to the concept of isometric embedding in metric spaces, and that
Gromov centrality can be broken down into a component that measures distance
and the residual centrality, which is based on the residual excess. We
investigate the properties of the residual centrality metric, such as its
non-negativity, maximum value, and symmetry, and discuss its relationship with
other centrality metrics. We also compare the values of the components of
Gromov centrality across various network types, including Erdos-Renyi, Barabasi-Albert, scale-free, and small-world networks, as well as biological and social network data sets.

Our research suggests that both precession of the perihelion and the shift of perihelion in planetary motion can be accounted for by an azimuthally symmetric gravitational field stemming from a spinning body. This approach also provides a simplified explanation for the phenomenon of frame dragging.

This research presents a new method for computing the Kronecker canonical form of a matrix pencil through a dynamical system approach, which utilizes flow fields to put the pencil into its canonical form through equivalence transformations. The developed algorithm has been implemented in the Julia programming language and is available on GitHub.

We investigate the T-duality relationship on torus bundles over almost abelian solvmanifolds, a class of spaces that includes nilmanifolds and Hopf manifolds. Our findings indicate that Topological T-duality holds for these torus bundles, revealing an extensive family of T-dual pairs.

Furthermore, a discrete version of the theory for non-compact connected invariant manifolds is established and applied to obtain new results for non-singular piecewise smooth monotone discrete-time systems.

We've developed a new method to model the electronic structure of molecules using a quantum computer. Our approach is based on the full configuration interaction method and uses a novel, iterative technique to find the most important configurations. To run this method on a quantum computer, we developed two new algorithms to apply the necessary transformations. Our new method has several advantages over existing techniques, including the ability to find excited states and to work with smaller quantum computers. We tested our method on a set of molecules and found that it can provide accurate results with fewer resources than existing techniques.

Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are widely used for learning data representations, but their performance is often limited by the mean-field assumption made during optimization. This assumption can lead to suboptimal results. A Deep Generative Decoder (DGD) has been proposed as an alternative approach that does not rely on this assumption. By using a deep neural network to model the posterior distribution, the DGD can achieve better results. This paper explores the potential of DGDs as a replacement for VAEs, and shows that they can be used in a variety of applications, including those with missing data. Theoretical analysis and experiments demonstrate that DGDs can provide better results than VAEs in many cases.

The presence of a primordial stochastic gravitational-wave background in the Universe's early stages can significantly alter its expansion history. This alteration may result in a measurable deficit in the number of large-scale structures observed. This phenomenon can also cause a discrepancy between predictions and observations of structures on the largest scales, known as the Baryon Acoustic Oscillation. This study investigates this discrepancy and demonstrates that a gravitational-wave background can resolve it. This resolution is achieved by adjusting the age of the Universe to match observations, while also reconciling predictions with observations of supernovae. This scenario is further supported by data from the Hubble Space Telescope and measurements of the expansion rate of the Universe. This discovery suggests that a deficit in the BAO scale on the largest scales may be attributed to a gravitational-wave background, which can also be constrained by further observations.
